reform_definition.free_hours: 15 hours a week of free childcare for every child from 9 months to school age, plus a further 15 hours where parents work and earn under £100,000 — replacing 30 hours for working parents under £100,000 and 15 hours for 3-4 year olds.
reform_definition.subsidy: A 75% subsidy of childcare costs for all, replacing Tax-Free Childcare's 25% top-up on parental spend capped at £2,000 a child. The Universal Credit childcare element is kept unchanged.

assumptions.margin: extensive (participation) and intensive (hours among parents in work); the hours elasticity is a total-hours effect, so the two overlap
assumptions.incidence: Free hours are valued at the DfE funding rate the model applies; the subsidy is valued at its cash value to the family.

comparable_costings.proposal: 15 hours free for all children 9 months to 4, with hours above that capped at 5% of family earnings
comparable_costings.source: New Economics Foundation, with Pregnant Then Screwed and JRF
comparable_costings.note: A whole-system package rather than an analogue of either leg: a 15-hour universal core plus a cap on the cost of further hours, replacing the funded-hours model and support through Universal Credit. NEF put it as initially cost-neutral at current usage, and £3-3.4bn net above the fully expanded funded-hours system at full expansion, at current provider rates. NEF says net costs fall by as much as 11% once more hours worked are allowed for.

comparable_costings.proposal: 30 hours for all 3-4 year olds, work test removed
comparable_costings.source: Sutton Trust and IFS (Farquharson), A Fair Start?
comparable_costings.note: Predates the under-3 expansion entirely, so it cannot be scaled to today's system, but it is the only IFS-authored costing of removing a work test. It is also a take-up anchor: £115m in the low take-up scenario and £560m in the high one, around the £250m central estimate — a range of nearly five times from the take-up of newly eligible families alone.

comparable_costings.proposal: The March 2023 expansion to under-3s, as originally costed
comparable_costings.source: HM Treasury and OBR, Spring Budget 2023
comparable_costings.note: Costed with about 60,000 entrants to employment by 2027-28, on a central estimate — the government's own labour supply assumption, and a cost anchor. Outturn ran above it on two separate measures: take-up was 26% above the December 2023 estimate by March 2025, and spending was about 28% above budget in 2024-25.

comparable_costings.proposal: Take-up of the 2023 expansion's new hours, by age
comparable_costings.source: Department for Education, Spring Budget 2023 policy costing note
comparable_costings.note: Not a costing of this reform but its take-up anchor. DfE costed the working-parent expansion on take-up of around 75% at age 2, 60% at age 1 and 35% at 9-12 months, from a range of 30-90% driven by parents' use of formal childcare. Those are working families; families outside work use less formal childcare.

comparable_costings.proposal: Universal 30 hours for 3-4 year olds, and options for 2-year-olds and a 20-hour core
comparable_costings.source: BCG for the Sutton Trust, Opportunity for All: technical appendix
comparable_costings.note: 2024-25 run costs. The 3-4 year old option applies take-up of about 45-75% by demographic group to children newly eligible, the 20-hour universal core with a 30-hour sliding subsidy 0-100%. Both ranges are driven mainly by the take-up assumption.

comparable_costings.proposal: One subsidy merging UC childcare support, Tax-Free Childcare and the 30 hours
comparable_costings.source: Early Education and Childcare Coalition, with the LSE
comparable_costings.note: The closest published analogue to the subsidy leg. The coalition reports the merged scheme could raise lower-income families' support without a comparable rise in spending at current take-up, and that support for low-income households would rise further if take-up improved. The summary page publishes no cost at higher take-up.

comparable_costings.source: IPPR (Statham, Parkes and Nanda), Towards a childcare guarantee
comparable_costings.note: Proposal-level paper; the cost is not restated here.

comparable_costings.proposal: Nordic-style universal childcare, 40 hours, 6 months to school age
comparable_costings.note: 40 hours a week, 48 weeks a year, from 6 months — an upper bound. The net range is small because WBG puts tax and benefit recoupment at 89-95% of gross. Gross and net are both from the 2017 costing; the 2020 Budget representation's £38-57bn gross range is not used, as pairing it with the 2017 net range would mix vintages.

ifs_free_childcare.label: Brewer, Cattan, Crawford and Rabe — Does more free childcare help parents work more?
ifs_free_childcare.description: England, 2005-2013. Regression discontinuity. Moving from 15 to 30-35 hours raised maternal participation 5.7pp and employment 3.5pp — about 12,000 more mothers a year — only where the youngest child was eligible. For every 570 free hours offered, only about 54 were additional care rather than care families already used — the rest displaced paid or informal care.

brewer_hours.label: Brewer, Cattan, Crawford and Rabe — Does more free childcare help parents work more? (IFS WP20/09)
brewer_hours.description: England. Table A.3 (file page 41): full-time eligibility raised mothers' usual weekly hours by 0.600 (s.e. 0.264), measured over all mothers with zeros for non-workers, against the Table 1 (file page 17) sample mean of 14.319 hours. The -0.042 hours elasticity used here is that +4.19% taken against a 100% price fall; the treatment was full-time eligibility (30-35 hours a week) relative to the part-time offer (12.5-15), file pages 8-9, not a 100% price fall. It is a total-hours effect that contains the participation channel, so it overlaps with the extensive-margin result.

akgunduz_plantenga.label: Akgunduz and Plantenga — Child care prices and maternal employment: a meta-analysis
akgunduz_plantenga.description: International meta-analysis, 43 estimates from 36 studies. Mean childcare price elasticity of maternal employment -0.277; Europe and Canada -0.19 against the US -0.35. Elasticities are smaller in high part-time countries like the UK, though that result holds only when sample year is excluded from the regression.

baker_gruber_milligan.label: Baker, Gruber and Milligan — Universal child care, maternal labor supply and family well-being
baker_gruber_milligan.description: Quebec, Canada. $5-a-day childcare raised married maternal participation 7.7pp, an implied cost elasticity of 0.236 the authors call low-end. Quebec offered up to 10 hours a day; England's entitlements are term-time and school-day, the main reason cited for weaker UK results.

dfe_30_hours_evaluation.label: DfE — Evaluation of the national rollout of 30 hours free childcare
dfe_30_hours_evaluation.description: England. Self-reported survey, not causal. Since starting the extended hours, 2% of mothers entered work and 26% raised their hours, against under 1% and 7% of fathers; reported impact was far higher for lower-income mothers (56% against 29%).

dfe_childcare_experiences.label: DfE — Expansion to early childcare entitlements: childcare experiences survey
dfe_childcare_experiences.description: England. The 2024-25 under-3s expansion has no causal evaluation yet. In the pilot wave 13% increased hours and 7% decreased, 78% unchanged. Self-reported, unweighted, 17% response rate.

de_henau.label: De Henau — Simulating employment and fiscal effects of universal childcare in the UK
de_henau.description: UK. UKMOD microsimulation with input-output multipliers: gross cost £26.6bn to £49.4bn a year, 61-72% recouped. Used here only as a ceiling — the employment response is assumed rather than estimated, part-time mothers are forced to full-time, and labour demand is assumed to absorb the supply in full.

obr_labour_supply.label: OBR — The impact of a NICs cut on labour supply
obr_labour_supply.description: UK. The participation elasticities used here, by gender, partner employment, age of youngest child and earnings quintile, and the Appendix E conversion to an elasticity with respect to the gain to work. Shipped in policyengine-uk as policyengine_uk.dynamics.participation.

bettendorf_jongen_muller.label: Bettendorf, Jongen and Muller — Childcare subsidies and labour supply
bettendorf_jongen_muller.description: Netherlands, CPB. A joint reform — childcare subsidies plus an earned income tax credit — raised maternal hours 6.2% against employment 3.0%, so the intensive margin moved about twice as much. Cited only for that ratio, which is why the participation-only estimate here is a floor: the two instruments are not separately identified, so neither level is transferable.

baseline_programmes.label: Universal entitlement (15 hours, 3-4 year olds)
baseline_programmes.official_spending_label: DfE £2.6bn, England, 2024-25, early years national funding formulae technical note (784,144 part-time equivalents)
baseline_programmes.official_caseload_label: DfE, January 2024: 778,327 registered excluding reception, working-parent children included
baseline_programmes.note: The comparator includes children on the working-parent entitlement, because policyengine-uk stacks the two: a working-parent child's first 15 hours are universal hours, and the working-parent entitlement pays only the hours above them. An earlier version of this row netted the 361,790 working-parent children off, which matched an engine that treated the schemes as alternatives. The model count is annual, so a child who starts reception in September still counts for the summer term, while the census is a January count that excludes reception, which is why the caseload ratio sits above the spending one. An earlier version of this row used £1.7bn from the dedicated schools grant allocations, which could not be reproduced; DfE's own technical note puts all universal hours at £2.6bn.

baseline_programmes.label: Working-parent entitlement (30 hours, under £100k)
baseline_programmes.official_spending_label: About £2.69bn, England, 2024-25, derived from DfE's early years national funding formulae technical note: £1.1bn of additional 3-4 year old hours, £0.94bn of the £1.5bn for 2-year-olds by part-time equivalents (200,571 of 321,335), and £0.65bn for under-2s
baseline_programmes.official_caseload_label: DfE, January 2025: 379,000 three- and four-year-olds plus 242,500 two-year-olds
baseline_programmes.note: The model's spending here is the working-parent hours above the universal and targeted hours each child already gets, not the full 30. The census is January 2025 but the model is read at 2024. January 2024 cannot serve this scheme — the two-year-old offer only began in April 2024, so that census misses half of it — while the model's own 2025 already contains the September 2025 expansion to 30 hours for under-threes, which the January 2025 census predates. Reading the model at 2025 against this figure gives 1.74x, against 1.39x at 2024, much of it that expansion. The mixed basis is a known limitation rather than a solved problem. DfE also warns that some two-year-olds eligible for both this and the disadvantaged offer were recorded here contrary to guidance, which moves children between this row and the next.

baseline_programmes.label: Disadvantaged two-year-old offer
baseline_programmes.note: Registrations have been falling year on year as the working-parent entitlement absorbs families who would previously have taken this offer, so the direction of travel is downward. The analysis runs on policyengine-uk 2.153.4, while Microcosm fitted this offer's take-up on 2.147.2; from 2.148.1 the engine tests the offer on Universal Credit earnings before the work allowance, which is stricter and lowers the modelled count.

baseline_programmes.label: Tax-Free Childcare
baseline_programmes.note: Both sides annual. HMRC also publishes a point-in-time monthly count; comparing an annual model aggregate against that stock manufactures a gap that is not there. This is the only programme here whose spending Microcosm is directly calibrated on, at 2025 against HMRC's later £599.8m.

subsidy_take_up.note: Both figures are the subsidy leg on its own, against the baseline fee base — not the combined run, where free hours displace some paid care first. They are comparable with each other and with the subsidy leg's static cost, and not with the combined total. Neither models new childcare use. The coded scope keeps Tax-Free Childcare's take-up, qualifying-child, provider and UK-connection rules and its exclusion of Universal Credit and tax-credit families; it removes the work test and the £100,000 cliff.

extended_entitlement_flag.note: The subsidy defined for would_claim_extended_childcare instead of would_claim_tfc, everything else as coded. Both flags are dataset inputs, uncorrelated with each other, and neither is estimated for this reform. On this data the extended flag is the lower of the two, so the switch reduces the leg and its response.

scope_scenarios.note: Combined runs, with free hours displacing paid care before the subsidy applies — not standalone legs added together, which overstates every scenario. Take-up and the exclusion of Universal Credit families are separate dimensions and are reported separately as well as together.

free_hours_take_up.note: Take-up of the new under-3 hours in England by families outside the working-parent hours. low: 60% of DfE's January 2026 take-up among working families by age (46% at 9-11 months, 76% at 1, 92% at 2). central: the 2-year-old offer's take-up flag. high: the dataset's universal flag, which Microcosm nests under the working-parent flag. Families on the working-parent hours keep the universal flag in every case. The rate is over children under 3 in those families and does not apply the usage draw, which also gates the hours.

subsidy_range.note: Static costs of the subsidy leg on its own. current_behaviour pays 75% only on the share of spend families route through a Tax-Free Childcare account today (tax_free_childcare_spend_routed_share); cma_fee_base rebases the under-5 fee base on the CMA residual (see fee_base_sensitivity); as_coded pays 75% of all reported spend for every family carrying the Tax-Free Childcare take-up flag, the full-take-up end.

implied_price_elasticity.note: Percentage change in employment among responding parents in work, over the percentage change in the out-of-pocket childcare price a potential entrant faces, central run. The central run applies the OBR participation elasticities unscaled; the price elasticities -0.05, -0.15 and -0.30 only set the ratio of the low and high bounds to it.

tax_free_childcare.population: benefit units with a child under 5, UK; flag only, before eligibility and usage

working_parent.population: benefit units with a child under 5, England; flag only, before eligibility and usage

universal.population: benefit units with a child under 5, England; flag only, before eligibility and usage

targeted.population: benefit units with a child under 5, England; flag only, before eligibility and usage

benchmarks.official_label: HMRC £632.2m top-ups to 1,085,020 children in 825,950 families, UK, 2024-25
benchmarks.note:
Model £0.579bn against HMRC's £632.2m at 2024 — 0.92x — on 1,146,058 children against 1,085,020, 1.06x. The average award is £505 against £583. That is the like-for-like comparison: same year, and children against children.

An earlier version of this file reported a 1.28x caseload gap and a 0.87x award, which was wrong on both counts. It set the model's 2027 benefit units against HMRC's 2025-26 *families*, mixing the entity and the year. HMRC publishes both counts for the same outturn — 825,950 families and 1,085,020 children in 2024-25 — so a model benefit-unit count divided by a family count is not a caseload ratio, and comparing across three years adds the caseload growth on top.

Microcosm UK 2024-25 calibrates Tax-Free Childcare on HMRC's March 2026 release at 2025 — £599.8m of top-ups to 1,151,515 children — and its build reports both within 0.2%. That is a later release and a later year than this row, so the two checks are not the same comparison.

benchmarks.official_label: DWP £611m, Great Britain, 2024-25 (a modelled element split of a measured UC total)
benchmarks.note:
Measured by abolishing it: the change in government spending when the 85% coverage rate is set to zero, at 2024 to match the published year. Summing uc_childcare_element instead gives £2.19bn, because it is a component of the UC maximum amount before the earnings taper — most of that face value never reaches a household.

Neither side is exact. DWP's £611m is a modelled split of a measured UC total: the workbook says element breakdowns are 'an estimate designed to be consistent with the OBR's Economic and Fiscal Outlook, although other credible breakdowns could be reached'. DWP's own caseload statistics do not reconcile with it either — 164,000 households at £400 a month implies about £790m.

On Microcosm the model costs the element at £0.67bn at 2024, with about 181,000 benefit units gaining from it against DWP's 164,000 to 177,000 households, at an average of £318 a month. Microcosm calibrates the count of households receiving the element at 2025 and carries an element-specific take-up flag (would_claim_uc_childcare). It does not affect this reform, which leaves the element unchanged.

benchmarks.official_label: ~£5.1bn residual, England, under-5s, 2025-26 — provider income less entitlement funding, which is parent fees *and other sources*
benchmarks.note: Derived, not published: the CMA estimates England's early years sector income at about £14bn in 2025-26, of which £8.9bn is funded entitlements, leaving about £5.1bn that parents pay providers. Both terms are the CMA's: the entitlements row above uses the IFS's £8.7bn for the same quantity, and mixing the two sources inside one subtraction would make the residual an artefact of the mismatch. On the IFS figure the residual would be £5.3bn and the gap 1.34x rather than 1.40x. That gross figure is the comparator. An earlier version of this check used £3.75bn, netting TFC and the UC childcare element off the residual — but childcare_expenses is the total fee and both of those are computed from it, so subtracting them double-counts the support and would overstate the gap as 1.90x rather than 1.40x. The CMA flags substantial uncertainty in the £14bn, and the residual on top of it is arithmetic rather than a published figure. Compared here against England under-5s only, which is what the benchmark covers; the model's full UK all-ages aggregate is shown separately below.

The full base the 75% subsidy applies to, since the subsidy reaches qualifying children up to 12. About three quarters is under-5s, a quarter school-age wraparound and holiday childcare, and the rest 12-plus. Only the under-5 England slice has a benchmark; no aggregate of school-age childcare spend is published by anyone, so that part is unchecked in either direction.

free_hours.label: 15 free hours for all from 9 months

fee_base_sensitivity.note: Only the under-5 slice is rebased, on the England benchmark of about £5.1bn of parent-paid fees; the school-age third of the base is left as modelled because nothing is published to rebase it against. The benchmark is gross of Tax-Free Childcare and the UC childcare element, matching childcare_expenses, which both are computed from. The CMA flags substantial uncertainty in the sector-income figure this derives from, and the residual also contains provider income that is not parent-paid fees. This is one fixed-quantity accounting scenario, not a lower bound: scenarios in the other direction, such as full take-up within the coded scope, exceed the headline.

An earlier version of this row netted the 361,790 working-parent children off, which matched an engine that treated the schemes as alternatives. The model count is annual, so a child who starts reception in September still counts for the summer term, while the census is a January count that excludes reception, which is why the caseload ratio sits above the spending one. An earlier version of this row used £1.7bn from the dedicated schools grant allocations, which could not be reproduced; DfE's own technical note puts all universal hours at £2.6bn.

baseline_programmes.label: Working-parent entitlement (30 hours, under £100k)
baseline_programmes.official_spending_label: About £2.69bn, England, 2024-25, derived from DfE's early years national funding formulae technical note: £1.1bn of additional 3-4 year old hours, £0.94bn of the £1.5bn for 2-year-olds by part-time equivalents (200,571 of 321,335), and £0.65bn for under-2s
baseline_programmes.official_caseload_label: DfE, January 2025: 379,000 three- and four-year-olds plus 242,500 two-year-olds
baseline_programmes.note: The model's spending here is the working-parent hours above the universal and targeted hours each child already gets, not the full 30. The census is January 2025 but the model is read at 2024. January 2024 cannot serve this scheme — the two-year-old offer only began in April 2024, so that census misses half of it — while the model's own 2025 already contains the September 2025 expansion to 30 hours for under-threes, which the January 2025 census predates. Reading the model at 2025 against this figure gives 1.74x, against 1.39x at 2024, much of it that expansion. The mixed basis is a known limitation rather than a solved problem. DfE also warns that some two-year-olds eligible for both this and the disadvantaged offer were recorded here contrary to guidance, which moves children between this row and the next.

baseline_programmes.label: Disadvantaged two-year-old offer
baseline_programmes.note: Registrations have been falling year on year as the working-parent entitlement absorbs families who would previously have taken this offer, so the direction of travel is downward. The analysis runs on policyengine-uk 2.153.4, while Microcosm fitted this offer's take-up on 2.147.2; from 2.148.1 the engine tests the offer on Universal Credit earnings before the work allowance, which is stricter and lowers the modelled count.

baseline_programmes.label: Tax-Free Childcare
baseline_programmes.note: Both sides annual. HMRC also publishes a point-in-time monthly count; comparing an annual model aggregate against that stock manufactures a gap that is not there. This is the only programme here whose spending Microcosm is directly calibrated on, at 2025 against HMRC's later £599.8m.

subsidy_take_up.note: Both figures are the subsidy leg on its own, against the baseline fee base — not the combined run, where free hours displace some paid care first. They are comparable with each other and with the subsidy leg's static cost, and not with the combined total. Neither models new childcare use. The coded scope keeps Tax-Free Childcare's take-up, qualifying-child, provider and UK-connection rules and its exclusion of Universal Credit and tax-credit families; it removes the work test and the £100,000 cliff.

extended_entitlement_flag.note: The subsidy defined for would_claim_extended_childcare instead of would_claim_tfc, everything else as coded. Both flags are dataset inputs, uncorrelated with each other, and neither is estimated for this reform. On this data the extended flag is the lower of the two, so the switch reduces the leg and its response.

scope_scenarios.note: Combined runs, with free hours displacing paid care before the subsidy applies — not standalone legs added together, which overstates every scenario. Take-up and the exclusion of Universal Credit families are separate dimensions and are reported separately as well as together.

free_hours_take_up.note: Take-up of the new under-3 hours in England by families outside the working-parent hours. low: 60% of DfE's January 2026 take-up among working families by age (46% at 9-11 months, 76% at 1, 92% at 2). central: the 2-year-old offer's take-up flag. high: the dataset's universal flag, which Microcosm nests under the working-parent flag. Families on the working-parent hours keep the universal flag in every case. The rate is over children under 3 in those families and does not apply the usage draw, which also gates the hours.

subsidy_range.note: Static costs of the subsidy leg on its own. current_behaviour pays 75% only on the share of spend families route through a Tax-Free Childcare account today (tax_free_childcare_spend_routed_share); cma_fee_base rebases the under-5 fee base on the CMA residual (see fee_base_sensitivity); as_coded pays 75% of all reported spend for every family carrying the Tax-Free Childcare take-up flag, the full-take-up end.

implied_price_elasticity.note: Percentage change in employment among responding parents in work, over the percentage change in the out-of-pocket childcare price a potential entrant faces, central run. The central run applies the OBR participation elasticities unscaled; the price elasticities -0.05, -0.15 and -0.30 only set the ratio of the low and high bounds to it.

tax_free_childcare.population: benefit units with a child under 5, UK; flag only, before eligibility and usage

working_parent.population: benefit units with a child under 5, England; flag only, before eligibility and usage

universal.population: benefit units with a child under 5, England; flag only, before eligibility and usage

targeted.population: benefit units with a child under 5, England; flag only, before eligibility and usage

benchmarks.official_label: HMRC £632.2m top-ups to 1,085,020 children in 825,950 families, UK, 2024-25
benchmarks.note:
Model £0.579bn against HMRC's £632.2m at 2024 — 0.92x — on 1,146,058 children against 1,085,020, 1.06x. The average award is £505 against £583. That is the like-for-like comparison: same year, and children against children.

An earlier version of this file reported a 1.28x caseload gap and a 0.87x award, which was wrong on both counts. It set the model's 2027 benefit units against HMRC's 2025-26 *families*, mixing the entity and the year. HMRC publishes both counts for the same outturn — 825,950 families and 1,085,020 children in 2024-25 — so a model benefit-unit count divided by a family count is not a caseload ratio, and comparing across three years adds the caseload growth on top.

Microcosm UK 2024-25 calibrates Tax-Free Childcare on HMRC's March 2026 release at 2025 — £599.8m of top-ups to 1,151,515 children — and its build reports both within 0.2%. That is a later release and a later year than this row, so the two checks are not the same comparison.

benchmarks.official_label: DWP £611m, Great Britain, 2024-25 (a modelled element split of a measured UC total)
benchmarks.note:
Measured by abolishing it: the change in government spending when the 85% coverage rate is set to zero, at 2024 to match the published year. Summing uc_childcare_element instead gives £2.19bn, because it is a component of the UC maximum amount before the earnings taper — most of that face value never reaches a household.

Neither side is exact. DWP's £611m is a modelled split of a measured UC total: the workbook says element breakdowns are 'an estimate designed to be consistent with the OBR's Economic and Fiscal Outlook, although other credible breakdowns could be reached'. DWP's own caseload statistics do not reconcile with it either — 164,000 households at £400 a month implies about £790m.

On Microcosm the model costs the element at £0.67bn at 2024, with about 181,000 benefit units gaining from it against DWP's 164,000 to 177,000 households, at an average of £318 a month. Microcosm calibrates the count of households receiving the element at 2025 and carries an element-specific take-up flag (would_claim_uc_childcare). It does not affect this reform, which leaves the element unchanged.

benchmarks.official_label: ~£5.1bn residual, England, under-5s, 2025-26 — provider income less entitlement funding, which is parent fees *and other sources*
benchmarks.note: Derived, not published: the CMA estimates England's early years sector income at about £14bn in 2025-26, of which £8.9bn is funded entitlements, leaving about £5.1bn that parents pay providers. Both terms are the CMA's: the entitlements row above uses the IFS's £8.7bn for the same quantity, and mixing the two sources inside one subtraction would make the residual an artefact of the mismatch. On the IFS figure the residual would be £5.3bn and the gap 1.34x rather than 1.40x. That gross figure is the comparator. An earlier version of this check used £3.75bn, netting TFC and the UC childcare element off the residual — but childcare_expenses is the total fee and both of those are computed from it, so subtracting them double-counts the support and would overstate the gap as 1.90x rather than 1.40x. The CMA flags substantial uncertainty in the £14bn, and the residual on top of it is arithmetic rather than a published figure. Compared here against England under-5s only, which is what the benchmark covers; the model's full UK all-ages aggregate is shown separately below.

The full base the 75% subsidy applies to, since the subsidy reaches qualifying children up to 12. About three quarters is under-5s, a quarter school-age wraparound and holiday childcare, and the rest 12-plus. Only the under-5 England slice has a benchmark; no aggregate of school-age childcare spend is published by anyone, so that part is unchecked in either direction.

free_hours.label: 15 free hours for all from 9 months

fee_base_sensitivity.note: Only the under-5 slice is rebased, on the England benchmark of about £5.1bn of parent-paid fees; the school-age third of the base is left as modelled because nothing is published to rebase it against. The benchmark is gross of Tax-Free Childcare and the UC childcare element, matching childcare_expenses, which both are computed from. The CMA flags substantial uncertainty in the sector-income figure this derives from, and the residual also contains provider income that is not parent-paid fees. This is one fixed-quantity accounting scenario, not a lower bound: scenarios in the other direction, such as full take-up within the coded scope, exceed the headline.
